text.content:
Harm and Recovery

You can catch your breath after a battle. You cannot always leave the battle behind. HP measures your immediate capacity to keep going. Grit gives you a limited reserve when you fall. Wounds record the lasting cost, even when their active penalties have been treated.

HP, healing and a safe breath

Subtract damage from current HP. Healing restores its printed amount, after any Life resistance, up to maximum HP. When the immediate danger has passed and you can safely take a breath, restore HP to full. The DA determines whether that pause is safe. A breath does not erase a wound or replenish spent Grit.

Deal with immediate conditions as the fiction permits. Companions can put out an ordinary fire when no danger prevents them from doing so. Poison, persistent injuries and other unresolved conditions do not all disappear because combat ended. Use each condition's removal rule. Resolve a Dying character's situation before leaving turn timing.

When you fall

Player characters enter Dying at 0 HP. Each entry causes a new wound. A creature or ordinary NPC normally dies at 0 HP; player-character survival procedures are not a second HP pool for every opponent.

Roll the new wound immediately. Roll three d6, plus one extra die for each prior wound, to a maximum of five dice total. Retain the highest three, sort them from lowest to highest, and read them as a three-digit number. Add the new scar to your wound count after determining this roll.

> Example — a second scar. You already have one wound, so roll four dice for > the next one. On 2, 4, 4, 6, keep 4, 4, 6: result 446. Read 446 on the appropriate > wound table. It is not a total of fourteen. Even after treatment, your earlier scar > still adds its die to this roll.

Choose the table for the damage type that dealt the most damage after resistance. You choose on a tie. Physical includes sonic and force. Fire, Cold and Lightning use Elemental wounds, but keep separate resistances. Mental, Radiant and Life/Necrotic have their own tables.

> Fully resisted components. If an event dealt only its minimum > 1 total damage because all components were reduced to zero, choose a wound table > from the event's original damage types. The player chooses which one applies.

If the listed body part is absent or the injury cannot apply, move to the next listed result until one does, such as 116 to 122. Do not reroll for a more convenient injury. The tables end at 666.

Your Dying turn

At the start of your turn while Dying, choose one Grit or a death roll. This choice stands for the turn; you cannot see the roll and then decide to spend Grit.

Spend one Grit to regain full HP. You retain the wound you just suffered. Otherwise, roll Fortitude and apply the death-roll result.

Death-roll resultEffect
WeakGain 1 death mark.
StandardNo change.
StrongStabilize at 0 HP and clear death marks.
Retained natural 111Gain 2 death marks instead of the ordinary Weak result.
Retained natural 666Restore 1 HP and clear death marks.

At three death marks, enter Last Words. Damage while already Dying adds one mark per damaging event; it does not create another wound. Damage that returns a stabilized character to Dying creates a new wound and adds one death mark.

A companion can use the universal Stabilize Maneuver. Stabilization clears death marks and leaves you at 0 HP, unable to act. Healing above 0 clears death marks and ends HP-caused unconsciousness. It does not necessarily remove another condition that also prevents action.

Last Words

A wound result of 666, or reaching three death marks, begins Last Words. You can speak, but do nothing else. You die at the end of the second following turn. Use that time for a farewell, a warning, a promise or silence. It belongs to the player.

Ordinary healing, treatment, potions and Grit cannot reverse Last Words. Only an explicit exceptional ability could say otherwise. Another character's ability may react to hearing those words without changing the finality of your death.

Treating a wound

A wound states its immediate effect, any lasting penalty, its required treatment and Recovery Value, or RV. Immediate pushes and knockdowns happen once. Temporary conditions decay under the condition rules. Lasting wound penalties remain until their stated remedy.

Use the appropriate treatment card: Soft Tissue, Bone, Mental, Elemental, Radiant or Life. Each attempt takes the card's full time. A wound can receive only one treatment attempt per day, across all healers. Weak, Standard and Strong add 1, 2 and 3 recovery progress. Keep accumulated progress with the wound.

When progress meets or exceeds RV, remove exactly the effects its remedy says it removes. The scar and accumulated wound count remain. Treatment does not regrow a missing limb. An artificial replacement or exceptional ability specifies the function it restores. Rest works as a remedy only when the wound explicitly lists it.

> Example — two different problems. Physical wound 333 applies Bleeding 1 and > a lasting Bane. Bleeding resolves and decays, or can be reduced with an appropriate > Main Action. It does not restart each turn because the scar exists. Soft Tissue > treatment must accumulate RV 3 to remove the lasting Bane. The scar still counts > on every later wound roll.

A cosmetic wound can need no treatment. If treating a socially significant scar removes its intimidation Boon and persuasion Bane, remove both, as printed. The DA decides when broad physical or mental activity penalties apply.

Read a condition

A numbered condition can use its rating for severity, duration, or both. At the end of the affected character's turn, resolve its effect, then reduce its temporary rating by 1. At 0 it ends. A condition gained during that turn also decreases at that turn's end.

An asterisk prevents automatic decay. Blinded 1 persists until its remedy; Blinded 2 would not make the blindness stronger. Record temporary and starred contributions separately. Add effective severity where relevant, but decay only the temporary part. Generic temporary reduction removes temporary rating; lasting treatment follows its source. Maintained Grappled and binary Prone have separate rules.

Dazed and Grappled determine your retained action categories at turn start. A change during the turn does not undo actions already spent or recalculate that turn's category selection. Grappled still prevents movement while the hold exists. Paralyzed, Asleep and Unconscious impose their immediate restrictions.

You can spend a Main Action to reduce Bleeding, Burning or Freezing on yourself or an adjacent creature by 1 with a plausible method. This is not a cure for every condition. Specialized cards may remove more or use a cheaper action.

> Example — resolve, then decay. Untreated Bleeding 3 deals 3 damage at turn end, > then becomes Bleeding 2. On later turns it deals 2 and then 1 before ending. > Reducing it with a Main Action before the first tick changes the sequence to 2, > then 1. Bleeding bypasses resistance; Burning and Freezing use matching resistance.

Asleep, Paralyzed, Unconscious and Petrified impose three defense Banes. Overlapping helpless states apply that penalty once. Dazed adds no defense Banes. Grappled gives attackers one Boon per rating of the actual target. When Dazed and Grappled overlap, use the greater action restriction, not their sum.
